title: Ποιμὴν καὶ θάλασσα
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 311. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ποιμὴν ἐν παραθαλασσίῳ τόπῳ ποίμνιον νέμων, ἑωρακὼς γαληνιῶσαν τὴν θάλατταν, ἐπεθύμησε πλεῦσαι πρὸς ἐμπορίαν.
sentences.tr: Poimēn en parathalassiōi topōi poimnion nemōn, heōrakōs galēniōsan tēn thalattan, epethymēse pleusai pros emporian.
sentences.l: A shepherd, pasturing a flock in a place beside the sea, having seen the sea lying calm, desired to sail for trade.
sentences.i: A shepherd who pastured his flock in a spot beside the sea, seeing the sea lying calm, took a longing to sail off on a trading venture.
sentences.n: ἑωρακώς is the perfect participle of ὁράω: the seeing is done and its effect stands, and it is that standing impression which sets the fable going. γαληνιάω is used of the sea, to lie calm. πρός with the accusative gives the end in view, 'with trade for its object'. The title prints θάλασσα, the body θάλατταν — the Attic -ττ- beside the commoner -σσ-, and both stand as printed.

sentences.t: Ἀπεμπολήσας οὖν τὰ πρόβατα καὶ φοινίκων βαλάνους πριάμενος ἀνήχθη.
sentences.tr: Apempolēsas oun ta probata kai phoinikōn balanous priamenos anēchthē.
sentences.l: So having sold off the sheep and having bought palm-acorns, he put out to sea.
sentences.i: So he sold off his sheep, bought a cargo of dates, and put out to sea.
sentences.n: φοινίκων βάλανοι, 'acorns of palms', is the ordinary Greek for dates; βάλανος names any nut-like fruit, and the palm's is a date. ἀνήχθη, aorist passive of ἀνάγω, is the standing term for putting out from harbour.

sentences.t: Χειμῶνος δὲ σφοδροῦ γενομένου καὶ τῆς νεὼς κινδυνευούσης βαπτίζεσθαι, πάντα τὸν φόρτον ἐκβαλὼν εἰς τὴν θάλατταν, μόλις κενῇ τῇ νηὶ διεσώθη.
sentences.tr: Cheimōnos de sphodrou genomenou kai tēs neōs kindyneuousēs baptizesthai, panta ton phorton ekbalōn eis tēn thalattan, molis kenēi tēi nēi diesōthē.
sentences.l: But a violent storm having come on and the ship being in danger of being sunk, having thrown all the cargo out into the sea, he was barely brought through safe with the ship empty.
sentences.i: But a violent storm came on and the ship was in danger of foundering, so he threw the whole cargo overboard and barely came through alive, with the ship empty.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes in succession — Χειμῶνος γενομένου and τῆς νεὼς κινδυνευούσης — set the circumstances before the main verb arrives; this stacking is the ordinary engine of the fables. βαπτίζομαι is to be dipped under, of a ship to founder. κενῇ τῇ νηί is a dative of attendant circumstance with the adjective thrown in front: 'with the ship, and it empty'.

sentences.t: Μετὰ δ’ ἡμέρας οὐκ ὀλίγας παριόντος τινὸς καὶ τῆς θαλάττης (ἔτυχε γὰρ αὕτη γαληνιῶσα) τὴν ἠρεμίαν θαυμάζοντος, ὑπολαβὼν οὗτος εἶπεν· « Ὦ λῷστε, φοινίκων αὖθις, ὡς ἔοικεν, ἐπιθυμεῖ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο φαίνεται ἡσυχάζουσα. »
sentences.tr: Meta d’ hēmeras ouk oligas pariontos tinos kai tēs thalattēs (etyche gar hautē galēniōsa) tēn ēremian thaumazontos, hypolabōn houtos eipen· « Ō lōiste, phoinikōn authis, hōs eoiken, epithymei, kai dia touto phainetai hēsychazousa. »
sentences.l: And after not a few days, someone passing by and marvelling at the stillness of the sea (for it happened to be lying calm), this man, taking-up-the-word, said: « My good fellow, it is craving palms again, so it seems, and for this reason it shows itself keeping quiet. »
sentences.i: Not many days later a passer-by was admiring the stillness of the sea — for it happened to be lying calm — and the shepherd took him up and said: « My good man, it is after dates again, so it seems, and that is why it is putting on this quiet. »
sentences.n: ὑπολαβών is the house rendering 'taking-up-the-word': the verb is answering, not seizing. φοινίκων stands alone here for the φοινίκων βάλανοι of the second sentence — 'palms' for the dates themselves. ἐπιθυμεῖ has the sea for its unnamed subject and takes up the shepherd's own ἐπεθύμησε in the first sentence; that is the joke — the calm is the sea's appetite, not its good nature. φαίνεται with the participle ἡσυχάζουσα states what the sea is plainly doing, not what it merely seems to do; φαίνομαι with an infinitive would give 'seems'. ὦ λῷστε, 'best of men', is a familiar and faintly condescending address. The round brackets here are Chambry's own parenthesis, not one of his editorial marks.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι τὰ παθήματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις μαθήματα γίνεται.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ta pathēmata tois anthrōpois mathēmata ginetai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that sufferings become lessons for men.
sentences.n: παθήματα beside μαθήματα — 'what is suffered' beside 'what is learnt' — is a proverbial jingle, and the same moral closes fable 183, which prints it with πολλάκις and with the plural γίνονται. γίνεται here is singular with a neuter plural subject, by the regular rule.
